lab_title: Vectors and 2D Projectile Motion in AR
top_level_objectives: Define 2D vectors in terms of magnitude and direction.
Perform 2D vector addition geometrically using the tip-to-tail method.
Resolve any 2D vector into horizontal and vertical components using right-triangle trigonometry.
Explain how 2D projectile motion consists of independent horizontal motion (constant velocity) and vertical motion (constant acceleration).
Analyze how changing the launch angle and initial speed alters the projectile's components, trajectory, range, and peak height.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the fundamental concept of a vector as a quantity possessing both magnitude and direction, contrasting it with scalar values.
key_visuals: A 3D vector arrow floating in the center of the room with an interactive grab-handle at its tip.
Dynamic digital readouts displaying the vector's magnitude (in meters) and direction (in degrees relative to a reference horizontal line).
A toggleable coordinate grid aligned with the real-world floor or table surface.
student_actions: Grab the tip of the vector arrow and drag it around the space to change its length and direction.
Observe how the real-time magnitude and angle values update as the arrow is manipulated.
Align the vector with a target angle and magnitude prompted by the system to test understanding.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the visual and mathematical process of adding two vectors together using the tip-to-tail method.
key_visuals: Two distinct vector arrows labeled Vector A (blue) and Vector B (green) resting on a virtual horizontal plane.
A dashed, grey shadow representation of Vector B to guide its movement.
A resultant vector arrow labeled Vector R (red) that dynamically updates when vectors are added.
student_actions: Grab Vector B and drag its tail to the tip of Vector A.
Observe how the resultant vector R automatically snaps into place from the tail of A to the tip of B.
Manipulate the directions of A and B while they are connected to observe how the resultant vector dynamically changes its magnitude and direction.

scenes.brief_purpose: Teach students how to decompose a 2D vector into orthogonal horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components using right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: A single vector V projected against a vertical 2D grid plane.
Dashed projection lines dropped from the tip of the vector to the x and y axes, forming a right-angled triangle.
Two component vectors, V_x along the horizontal axis and V_y along the vertical axis.
Live trigonometric formulas (V_x = V cos(theta) and V_y = V sin(theta)) that update mathematically as the vector changes.
student_actions: Drag the tip of vector V to change its angle and magnitude.
Observe how the component vectors V_x and V_y shrink and grow in response to the changing angle.
Tap on the cos(theta) and sin(theta) terms in the formula to highlight the corresponding adjacent/opposite sides of the virtual right triangle.

scenes.scene_name: The Projectile Launcher: Decomposing Initial Velocity
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply vector decomposition to a physical scenario by setting up a virtual projectile launcher and analyzing its initial velocity vector.
key_visuals: A virtual tabletop launcher (cannon) that can be rotated to adjust the launch angle.
An initial velocity vector arrow (V_0) emerging from the muzzle of the launcher.
Decomposed component arrows V_0x (horizontal) and V_0y (vertical) displayed at the launcher's muzzle.
student_actions: Adjust the angle of the launcher and the initial launch speed using virtual sliders.
Observe how increasing the angle increases V_0y but decreases V_0x, and vice versa.
Press the 'Launch' button to fire a low-speed test projectile and watch it follow a parabolic path.

scenes.scene_name: Independence of Motion: Tracking Components in Flight
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the independence of horizontal and vertical motion by tracking the velocity components during a slow-motion flight.
key_visuals: A projectile moving in slow motion along its parabolic trajectory.
A real-time vector overlay attached to the flying projectile, showing the total velocity vector, the horizontal velocity component vector (V_x), and the vertical velocity component vector (V_y).
Strobe-like ghost frames of the projectile dropped at equal time intervals, showing equal horizontal spacing but unequal vertical spacing.
student_actions: Use a playback slider to scrub forward and backward through the projectile's flight.
Observe that the horizontal velocity vector (V_x) remains constant in length and direction throughout the entire flight because there is no horizontal force.

Observe that the vertical velocity vector (V_y) decreases on the way up, momentarily becomes zero at the peak of the trajectory, and increases in the downward direction on the way down due to gravity.

scenes.scene_name: Launch Sandbox: Optimizing Range and Height
scenes.brief_purpose: Provide an interactive sandbox where students manipulate variables to find the relationships between launch parameters, trajectory shape, range, and maximum height.
key_visuals: A customizable launch zone with a target placed at a distance on the floor.
Persistent, color-coded trajectory paths left behind by previous launches for easy comparison.
A dynamic data table recording launch angle, initial speed, V_0x, V_0y, maximum height, and total range for each trial.
student_actions: Experiment with launching the projectile at different angles (e.g., 30, 45, and 60 degrees) while keeping the launch speed constant.
Analyze the trajectory paths to discover that a 45-degree launch angle yields the maximum range, and explain this in terms of the balance between V_0x and V_0y.
Complete a challenge to hit a target placed at a specific distance and height by calculating and setting the correct initial velocity components.
